extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Apply the USPTO 2019 PEG (and October 2019 Update) to determine 35 U.S.C. §101 subject-matter eligibility for life-sciences and data-processing claims using the Step 1 / Step 2A / Step 2B framework and associated considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1: Statutory Category (Is the claim to a statutory class?)
rubrics_metrics.description: This part of the eligibility analysis evaluates whether the claim falls within any statutory category (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter). See MPEP 2106.03.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim recites at least one step or act (e.g., calculating a ratio, administering a drug), it can be a process. If it recites a combination of concrete devices (memory, processor, reader) it can be a machine. (Example: 'The claim recites at least one step or act, including calculating a ratio. Thus, the claim is to a process...')

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One: Does the claim 'recite' a judicial exception?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim sets forth or describes a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, product of nature). A claim 'recites' an exception when the exception is set forth or described in the claim. See MPEP 2106.04(II) and October 2019 Update.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify specific claim limitations that align with exception categories; multiple exceptions may be present in a single limitation. It is sufficient to identify that a limitation aligns with at least one judicial exception to proceed to further analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract Idea Groupings (mathematical concepts; mental processes; certain methods of organizing human activity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract ideas are grouped to include mathematical concepts (e.g., calculations), mental processes (acts that can be performed in the human mind), and certain methods of organizing human activity (fundamental economic practices, managing interactions, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple arithmetic (division) or calculations are mathematical concepts. Mental processes include evaluations and comparisons that humans perform (e.g., comparing current behavior to past behavior). Reciting the use of a generic physical aid (pen, calculator) does not negate the mental nature. If a limitation requires arithmetic calculation or mental evaluation, classify it under the relevant abstract-idea grouping and proceed to Step 2A Prong Two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Nature / Product of Nature exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite natural relationships (e.g., a correlation between biomarkers and a disease), naturally occurring products, or products found in nature may implicate law of nature or product of nature exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a claim describes a naturally occurring relationship (e.g., ratio of C11 to C13 indicates non-responder phenotype) treat as a law of nature; where it claims nature-based products evaluate under product-of-nature analysis (markedly different characteristics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly Different Characteristics analysis for nature-based products
rubrics_metrics.description: For product claims reciting nature-based product limitations, evaluate whether the claimed product has markedly different characteristics from what exists in nature; if not, it may be a product-of-nature exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General rule: for process claims, the markedly different analysis is not performed for nature-based products used in the process (MPEP 2106.04(c)(I)(C)), unless the process claim is drafted so it is no different in substance than a product claim. Decide whether the claim is focused on products per se or on a process using natural products; apply markedly-different analysis accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two: Integration into a Practical Application
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claim as a whole integrates the recited judicial exception into a practical application by identifying additional elements beyond the exception and assessing those elements individually and in combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 2019 PEG Section III(A)(2) analysis: additional elements that impose meaningful limits on the exception (e.g., particular treatment tied to identified phenotype, operation of a machine based on the exception) may integrate the exception. Do not consider whether limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional in this prong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular Treatment or Prophylaxis consideration (integration prong)
rubrics_metrics.description: A treatment or prophylaxis that is particular to an identified patient phenotype can integrate an exception into a practical application (i.e., a claim using an exception to identify patients and then administering a particular treatment is not 'directed to' the exception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claim requires administering a specific therapeutic agent or a treatment particular to the identified phenotype (e.g., non-steroidal agent, rapamycin, plasmapheresis), that limitation can have more than a nominal relationship to the judicial exception and support eligibility (see Vanda, Endo). The treatment limitation must meaningfully limit the abstract idea (not be wholly generic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular Machine consideration (integration prong)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recitation of a particular machine or device that meaningfully applies the exception may integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the machine limitation is more than a generic recitation of a known device used for its conventional purpose. A specific machine that performs steps in a particular manner or improves technology is more likely to integrate the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular Transformation consideration (integration prong)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed transformation of a thing in a particular way that meaningfully applies the exception may integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the transformation is particular and concrete (not merely incidental or conventional) and whether it imposes meaningful limits beyond abstract idea/math.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other Meaningful Limitations (integration prong)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that use the information produced by the judicial exception to take corrective action or effect a concrete change (e.g., automatically operating a gate to route animals) can integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: automating a sorting gate based on analyzed animal behavior uses the abstract idea to operate a physical device and thus can be an 'other meaningful limitation' that practically applies the exception (see livestock sorting example). Consider whether the limitation avoids mere automation of human tasks and instead uses the information to effect a concrete, meaningful action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere Instructions To Apply An Exception (negative indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: High-level, generic directions to apply an exception (equivalent to adding the words 'apply it') do not integrate the exception into a practical application and cannot supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the treatment step or other additional element merely tells practitioners to 'apply' the calculation or law without specifying how, it is nominal and will not save eligibility (Mayo). Rejections should explain that the additional element is at best the equivalent of 'apply it'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant Extra-Solution Activity (negative indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extra activities that are conventional, insignificant, or do no meaningful work beyond the exception do not integrate the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data-gathering steps, mere use of generic computer components, or other routine activities recited at a high level of generality are often insignificant extra-solution activity and do not make claim eligible under 2A Prong Two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-of-Use and Technological Environment limitations (token limitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting an abstract idea to a particular field of use (e.g., livestock management, commodities markets) is typically a token or mere recitation of field and does not make a claim patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Bilski: merely identifying the participants or field does little more than describe how the abstract idea could be used; treat such limitations skeptically as they often do not meaningfully limit the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements to Functioning of a Computer or Other Technology
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element that improves computer functionality or other technology can integrate an abstract idea into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between using a computer as a tool to automate a mental process (insufficient) versus improving the computer itself or enabling a technological improvement. Case law (e.g., Trading Technologies) provides examples where providing more information to facilitate trading did not improve computer functionality; examiners should identify concrete technological improvements when present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B: 'Inventive Concept' — Does the claim add 'significantly more' than the exception?
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is directed to a judicial exception after Step 2A, evaluate whether any additional elements, individually or in combination, add something significantly more than the judicial exception (an 'inventive concept'). See MPEP 2106.05.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether additional elements are more than conventional or routine; mere instructions to apply an exception or nominal post-solution activity cannot satisfy 2B. If no inventive concept is present, claim is ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-Understood, Routine, Conventional (WURC) Activity (Step 2B consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether additional claim elements are well-understood, routine, and conventional; if they are, they cannot supply an inventive concept under Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WURC analysis is excluded from Step 2A Prong Two but is applicable in Step 2B. For example, if administering a conventional therapy is routine in the field, that fact is relevant to whether the claim amounts to significantly more than the exception under 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Interpretation: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim terms are presumed to have their plain meaning consistent with the specification as interpreted by a person of ordinary skill in the art (MPEP 2111).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use BRI when determining what the claim 'recites' for eligibility analysis. The BRI may encompass multiple embodiments and can affect whether limitations are considered meaningful or nominal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wherein Clauses and Functional Language carry patentable weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations found in wherein clauses or recited functionally are not automatically disregarded; they can impose patentable weight if the specification supports them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ignore 'wherein' clauses — they may limit claim scope (e.g., specifying rapamycin or a non-steroidal agent). Examine written description support (MPEP 2163) for genus/functionally claimed limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble and Intended Use (when preamble limits claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: A preamble does not limit a claim unless it positively adds a limitation or is necessary to give meaning to claim body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the preamble only indicates an intended use (e.g., 'for use in monitoring the health of dairy livestock'), it generally does not add limitations absent positive limiting language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contingent Limitations and Multi-Embodiment Coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Contingent limitations (conditional steps) can cause claims to encompass multiple alternative embodiments under BRI; prior art need only teach one embodiment to anticipate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a claim contains contingent actions (if A do X, if B do Y), the claim's BRI may include three or more embodiments. Examiners should be aware that anticipation can be established by references disclosing any single encompassed embodiment (see MPEP 2111.04(II)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Generic Computer/Processor does not negate a mental-process abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting a processor or generic computer components that carry out mental processes or calculations does not necessarily avoid the abstract-idea exception; the computer may be treated as a tool automating human mental steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim merely uses the computer to perform what humans can do mentally or is recited at a high level of generality using generic components, treat it as automating an abstract idea unless the claim recites a technological improvement in the computer itself or a particular machine implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying the Exception in a Rejection (practice note)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection should identify the specific claim limitation(s) that recite the judicial exception and explain why those limitations constitute an abstract idea, law of nature, or product of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how the limitation aligns with an exception (e.g., limitation (a) recites a mathematical calculation) and then explain why additional elements fail to integrate the exception or provide an inventive concept. Include citations to MPEP sections and relevant case law (Mayo, Vanda, Endo, Bilski, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice note: Consider all statutory requirements during examination (written description, novelty, obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a claim is analyzed for eligibility under §101, examiners should also evaluate each claim for compliance with other statutory requirements (definiteness, written description, novelty, non-obviousness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a functionally claimed genus ('non-steroidal agent capable of treating NAS-3') may raise written description support issues (MPEP 2163). Also consider applicant-admitted statements as prior art (MPEP 2129(I)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Token Limitation vs. Meaningful Limitation (how to distinguish)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between limitations that are merely token or nominal (do not meaningfully limit an abstract idea) and those that impose a meaningful restriction or application of the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Token limitations include generic field-of-use statements or 'apply it' language. Meaningful limitations include particular treatments, machine operations that effect physical change, or steps that improve the functioning of technology. Evaluate whether the limitation 'uses' the abstract idea to impose a meaningful limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Bright Lines Between Exception Types (practical guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no bright-line rules separating types of judicial exceptions; identifying that a limitation aligns with at least one exception is sufficient to continue analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A limitation may be characterized as a mathematical concept, a mental process, and a law of nature simultaneously; examiners should identify an applicable exception and proceed with the multi-step analysis rather than searching for exclusive categorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automation of Human Tasks is Generally Insufficient (when using computers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely automating tasks previously performed by humans via generic computing does not by itself confer eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If additional elements only automate human mental processes using generic computer components without improving computer functionality or imposing meaningful limits, treat as ineligible unless there is a demonstrated technological improvement or other meaningful limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples Are Illustrative and Fact-Specific (use with 2019 PEG)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office's examples are hypothetical, illustrating claim analysis under the 2019 PEG and Issue Spotting Chart; different fact patterns may yield different eligibility outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not require a claim to mirror an example to be eligible; interpret examples based on their fact patterns and apply the 2019 PEG guidance to the claim at hand. Use broadest reasonable interpretation and cite appropriate MPEP and case law references when applying the examples.
